questions.stem: The overall equation of PHOTOSYNTHESIS is:
questions.explanation: PHOTOSYNTHESIS — process by which GREEN PLANTS + algae + cyanobacteria convert LIGHT ENERGY into CHEMICAL ENERGY (glucose). OVERALL EQUATION: 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O + LIGHT ENERGY → C₆H₁₂O₆ (glucose) + 6 O₂ (catalysed by CHLOROPHYLL in chloroplasts). LOCATION: CHLOROPLAST of leaf MESOPHYLL CELLS (especially palisade mesophyll). CHLOROPLAST has: (a) THYLAKOID membrane stacked as GRANA — site of LIGHT-DEPENDENT reactions; (b) STROMA (fluid) — site of LIGHT-INDEPENDENT (CALVIN) cycle. TWO PHASES: (1) LIGHT REACTIONS (Hill reaction, 1937) — in thylakoid membrane; photolysis of WATER: 2H₂O → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ + O₂ (oxygen is BY-PRODUCT); energy captured as ATP + NADPH via Photosystem I + II + ETC (electron transport chain). (2) DARK REACTIONS / CALVIN CYCLE (Calvin-Benson-Bassham, 1950; Nobel 1961) — in stroma; CO₂ fixed by RuBisCO (world's most abundant enzyme) to form 3-PGA, reduced to G3P using ATP + NADPH, eventually combined into glucose. GLOBAL SIGNIFICANCE: photosynthesis produces ~320 billion tonnes of O₂/yr; underpins ALL food chains; counters atmospheric CO₂ (limits CO₂ rise from fossil fuels, partially). CO₂ level ~420 ppm (April 2025, NOAA Mauna Loa) vs pre-industrial 280 ppm. 'Net Primary Productivity' (NPP) = photosynthesis - plant respiration. OCEANIC (marine) photosynthesis by PHYTOPLANKTON (diatoms + cyanobacteria) contributes ~50% of global O₂. NITROGEN FIXATION is a separate process (by Rhizobium + free-living bacteria), not part of photosynthesis.

questions.stem: CHLOROPHYLL, the green pigment essential for photosynthesis, is located in:

options.option_text: THYLAKOID membranes within CHLOROPLASTS — specifically as part of Photosystem I + II complexes

questions.explanation: CHLOROPHYLL — green pigment that absorbs LIGHT for photosynthesis. LOCATION: embedded in the THYLAKOID MEMBRANE of CHLOROPLASTS, organised as LIGHT-HARVESTING COMPLEXES of Photosystem I (PSI) + Photosystem II (PSII). STRUCTURE: porphyrin ring with Mg²⁺ at centre (hence Mg-deficient plants yellow); long phytol tail anchors it in membrane. TYPES: (a) CHLOROPHYLL A — the primary pigment, absorbs RED (660nm) + BLUE-VIOLET (430nm); key reaction centre molecule. (b) CHLOROPHYLL B — accessory pigment; absorbs different wavelengths, transfers energy to Chl a. Ratio Chl a:Chl b = 3:1 typically. (c) CHLOROPHYLLS c, d, e, f — in algae + some bacteria. OTHER PLANT PIGMENTS: (1) CAROTENOIDS — orange (carotene) + yellow (xanthophyll) accessory pigments; absorb blue-green wavelengths; protect from photo-oxidation; visible in autumn leaves + carrots (beta-carotene = vitamin A precursor). (2) ANTHOCYANINS — reds, purples, blues (red cabbage, blueberries); pH-sensitive (natural indicators). (3) BETALAINS — beetroot red. LIGHT ABSORPTION: chlorophyll REFLECTS GREEN — hence plants appear green. Most active at RED (~660-680 nm) + BLUE (~430-460 nm). If under green LED light, plants struggle to photosynthesise. WHY LEAVES TURN YELLOW IN AUTUMN: chlorophyll degrades faster, revealing underlying carotenoids (always present). RUBISCO is the ENZYME (ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase), not a pigment — it's in the STROMA.

questions.stem: The oxygen released during photosynthesis COMES FROM:

options.option_text: Water (H₂O) — proven by Ruben + Kamen (1941) isotope-labelling experiment using ¹⁸O

questions.explanation: OXYGEN origin in photosynthesis — WATER, not CO₂. PROOF: classic experiment by SAMUEL RUBEN + MARTIN KAMEN (1941, UC Berkeley) using ISOTOPE LABELLING with ¹⁸O (oxygen-18 heavy isotope). They labelled (a) water with ¹⁸O (H₂¹⁸O) — oxygen released by plant was ¹⁸O₂; (b) CO₂ with ¹⁸O (C¹⁸O₂) — oxygen released was ordinary ¹⁶O₂. CONCLUSION: O₂ released comes from WATER split (photolysis), not from CO₂. This settled a century-old debate. PHOTOLYSIS of water happens at the oxygen-evolving complex (OEC) of Photosystem II: 2H₂O → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ + O₂↑. The OEC contains a Mn₄CaO₅ cluster (one of the most studied enzyme centres in biochem). EVOLUTIONARY SIGNIFICANCE: oxygenic photosynthesis first evolved in cyanobacteria ~2.4-2.7 Ga ago (BYA). The 'GREAT OXIDATION EVENT' (GOE, ~2.4 Ga) oxygenated Earth's atmosphere + oceans, causing mass extinction of anaerobes but paving the way for aerobic life + eukaryotes. OXYGEN atmospheric level today = 21% (was near 0% pre-GOE, peaked at 35% during Carboniferous 300 Ma, then stabilised). ENDOSYMBIOTIC THEORY (Lynn Margulis, 1967): CHLOROPLASTS evolved from engulfed cyanobacteria — supported by their double membrane, circular DNA, 70S ribosomes, division by binary fission. Similarly MITOCHONDRIA evolved from engulfed aerobic proteobacteria. Stromatolites (fossil cyanobacterial mats in Australia, Canada, India) provide earliest evidence — ~3.5 Ga.

questions.stem: The enzyme RuBisCO, central to the Calvin cycle, fixes:

options.option_text: CO₂ — attaches CO₂ to a 5-carbon sugar (RuBP), forming two 3-carbon molecules (3-PGA); most abundant protein on Earth

questions.explanation: RuBisCO (RIBULOSE-1,5-BISPHOSPHATE CARBOXYLASE/OXYGENASE) — the ENZYME that catalyses the FIRST step of the CALVIN CYCLE (carbon fixation). Reaction: CO₂ + RuBP (5-C) → 2 molecules of 3-PGA (3-phosphoglycerate, 3-C each) via unstable 6-C intermediate. FEATURES: (1) LARGE + SLOW — catalyses only ~3 reactions per second (most enzymes: 1000s/sec) — so plants need ENORMOUS QUANTITIES. (2) Plants contain ~50% of their leaf protein as RuBisCO — RuBisCO is often called 'THE MOST ABUNDANT PROTEIN ON EARTH' (total biomass ~0.7 Gt). (3) HAS a DUAL function — can also OXYGENATE RuBP (react with O₂ instead of CO₂) leading to PHOTORESPIRATION — a wasteful process that releases CO₂ + consumes ATP. Photorespiration is WORSENED by hot + dry conditions. PLANTS have evolved WORKAROUNDS: (a) C4 PLANTS — CO₂ concentrated in bundle-sheath cells (Hatch-Slack pathway, 1966); examples = maize, sugarcane, sorghum, bajra, amaranth — enzyme PEP carboxylase first fixes CO₂ into oxaloacetate, shuttled to bundle sheath where RuBisCO acts; photorespiration suppressed; advantage in hot climates. (b) CAM PLANTS (Crassulacean Acid Metabolism) — stomata OPEN AT NIGHT (to conserve water), CO₂ stored as malate in vacuole, released to RuBisCO by day; plants: cactus, pineapple, agave, some orchids; advantage in desert climates. (c) C3 plants (most common — wheat, rice, soyabean, potato) — standard Calvin cycle; less efficient in heat. C4 + CAM are climate-adaptation evolutionary innovations ~30 Mya + ~80 Mya respectively.

questions.stem: Which scientist is considered the DISCOVERER of photosynthesis by showing plants produce oxygen?

options.option_text: JAN INGENHOUSZ (1779) — showed that only GREEN parts of plants + only in SUNLIGHT produce O₂

questions.explanation: DISCOVERY of PHOTOSYNTHESIS — piecewise over ~200 years: (1) 1648 — JAN BAPTISTA VAN HELMONT (Belgian) — grew willow in weighed pot; after 5 years, tree gained 74 kg, soil lost only 57g; concluded WATER was source of plant mass (partially right!). (2) 1771 — JOSEPH PRIESTLEY (English, also discovered oxygen) — mint plant + candle experiment: plants 'restore' air (O₂) spoiled by burning candles. (3) 1779 — JAN INGENHOUSZ (Dutch) — showed plants produce O₂ ONLY IN SUNLIGHT + ONLY GREEN PARTS do it. Published 'Experiments upon Vegetables'. Founded the field. (4) 1796 — JEAN SENEBIER (Swiss) — showed CO₂ is consumed + O₂ released. (5) 1804 — NICOLAS-THÉODORE DE SAUSSURE — added WATER as raw material (quantified balance). (6) 1845 — JULIUS ROBERT MAYER — established that plants convert SOLAR ENERGY into chemical energy. (7) 1860 — JULIUS SACHS — showed GLUCOSE/STARCH is the product. (8) 1937 — ROBERT HILL — chloroplasts alone (in isolation) can produce O₂ when given light + electron acceptor (HILL REACTION). (9) 1941 — RUBEN + KAMEN — ¹⁸O tracer: O₂ comes from water, not CO₂. (10) 1945-57 — MELVIN CALVIN (UC Berkeley) — worked out the carbon pathway (Calvin cycle) using radioactive ¹⁴C tracing; awarded Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1961. (11) 1961 — PETER MITCHELL — CHEMIOSMOTIC THEORY for ATP synthesis (Nobel 1978). Photosynthesis is thus a classic case of INCREMENTAL scientific discovery over centuries.

questions.stem: The small openings on the underside of leaves through which CO₂ enters + O₂ + water vapour exit are called:

options.option_text: STOMATA (singular: stoma) — flanked by GUARD CELLS that open/close the aperture based on turgor pressure

questions.explanation: STOMATA (Greek 'mouths') — tiny pores on plant EPIDERMIS, mainly on the UNDERSIDE of leaves (to reduce evaporation). DENSITY ~10,000-1,00,000 per cm² on leaf underside. Each stoma is flanked by two specialised kidney-shaped GUARD CELLS that regulate opening. FUNCTIONS: (1) gas exchange — CO₂ enters for photosynthesis; O₂ exits. (2) TRANSPIRATION — water vapour exits (pulling water up from roots — TRANSPIRATION PULL, essential for xylem sap flow). STOMATAL OPENING MECHANISM: (a) in LIGHT, guard cells actively pump K⁺ ions in, lowering water potential; (b) water enters by osmosis → guard cells SWELL (turgid) → cell walls bow outward (thicker inner walls, thinner outer) → APERTURE OPENS. (c) at NIGHT / drought, K⁺ pumped out, guard cells shrink, aperture CLOSES. HORMONE: ABSCISIC ACID (ABA) — closes stomata under drought stress. CAM PLANTS (cacti, pineapple) — reverse the cycle: open stomata at NIGHT to conserve water in desert conditions. STOMATA + CLIMATE: (a) high atm CO₂ → plants can partially close stomata, conserving water — one reason fertilisation effect of rising CO₂ is real but nuanced. (b) STOMATAL DENSITY in fossil leaves is used to reconstruct past atm CO₂ levels. LENTICELS are similar pores on woody stems + bark — for gas exchange in stems. HYDATHODES — water-release pores at leaf margins (GUTTATION, water droplets at leaf tips in dew). In AQUATIC plants, stomata on UPPER surface (reversed); in xerophytes, stomata in SUNKEN pits with hairs to reduce water loss.

questions.stem: Which wavelength region of visible light is MOST EFFECTIVELY USED in photosynthesis?

options.option_text: BLUE (~430-460 nm) + RED (~660-680 nm) — peaks absorbed by chlorophyll; GREEN is largely REFLECTED (hence leaves look green)

questions.explanation: PHOTOSYNTHETICALLY ACTIVE RADIATION (PAR) — wavelengths 400-700 nm (roughly = visible light) used for photosynthesis. ABSORPTION MAXIMA of chlorophylls + accessory pigments: (a) CHLOROPHYLL A: 430 nm (blue) + 662 nm (red); (b) CHLOROPHYLL B: 453 nm (blue) + 642 nm (orange-red); (c) CAROTENOIDS: 400-500 nm (blue); (d) PHYCOBILINS (in cyanobacteria + red algae): 620-650 nm + 560 nm. GREEN LIGHT (~500-570 nm) is LEAST ABSORBED — mostly REFLECTED + transmitted (why leaves appear green to us). This is slight waste — plants could have evolved to use green; some algae + forest-floor plants do (phycobilin-rich). ENGELMANN EXPERIMENT (1882) — T. Engelmann split light into a spectrum + fed it onto a strand of SPIROGYRA algae in a solution with aerobic bacteria. BACTERIA CLUSTERED at the red + blue regions where O₂ was produced most — confirming the ACTION SPECTRUM of photosynthesis matches chlorophyll absorption. CO₂ + TEMPERATURE + LIGHT INTENSITY are the three main EXTERNAL limiting factors (Blackman 1905, 'Law of Limiting Factors' — whichever is in shortest supply limits rate). LIGHT COMPENSATION POINT — intensity at which net photosynthesis = net respiration (no net O₂); lower for shade plants. LIGHT SATURATION POINT — beyond which more light doesn't increase rate (RuBisCO becomes limiting). SUPPLEMENTAL LED grow-lights are usually BLUE + RED (purple-pink spectrum) for this reason — maximum efficiency.

questions.stem: C4 plants (like MAIZE, SUGARCANE, SORGHUM) are MORE EFFICIENT than C3 plants in:

options.option_text: HOT + DRY climates with high light intensity — they minimise photorespiration by concentrating CO₂ around RuBisCO

questions.explanation: C4 PHOTOSYNTHESIS — discovered by HATCH + SLACK (Australia, 1966) while studying sugarcane. NAMED 'C4' because first stable product is a 4-CARBON compound (oxaloacetate → malate), unlike 'C3' where first product is 3-carbon 3-PGA. PATHWAY: (1) CO₂ first fixed by PEP CARBOXYLASE (has VERY HIGH affinity for CO₂, so works even at low CO₂) in MESOPHYLL cells → forms OAA (oxaloacetate, 4C). (2) OAA converted to MALATE. (3) Malate shuttled to BUNDLE-SHEATH cells (which surround vascular tissue in KRANZ anatomy). (4) Malate decarboxylated there, releasing CO₂ at HIGH concentration near RUBISCO. (5) RuBisCO carries out Calvin cycle as usual, but photorespiration is SUPPRESSED by the high local CO₂. ADVANTAGES: (1) MUCH LESS photorespiration — so better efficiency at high temp + light intensity. (2) Higher WATER-USE EFFICIENCY (WUE) — can keep stomata partly closed. (3) Higher NUE (nitrogen-use efficiency). DISADVANTAGE: higher energy cost (extra ATP). EXAMPLES of C4 plants: MAIZE (corn), SUGARCANE, SORGHUM (jowar), PEARL MILLET (bajra), AMARANTH, some CRABGRASSES. C3 plants (most — rice, wheat, soyabean, cotton, potato) dominate temperate + cooler climates. CAM PLANTS (Crassulacean Acid Metabolism) — similar CO₂-concentration mechanism BUT stomata OPEN AT NIGHT only (for water conservation in deserts); include cacti, pineapple, agave, some orchids, succulents. Only ~3% of plant species are C4; but contribute ~23% of global terrestrial photosynthesis (concentrated in grasslands + tropical crops). Research to engineer C4 rice is ongoing (C4 Rice Project).

questions.stem: The food PRODUCED in photosynthesis is stored by MOST PLANTS primarily as:

options.option_text: STARCH — a polymer of glucose; stored in amyloplasts of roots, tubers, seeds + leaves (transient starch)

questions.explanation: STARCH — the primary storage CARBOHYDRATE in plants; polymer of α-D-glucose. TWO components: (1) AMYLOSE (20-25%) — linear α-1,4 glucose chains, helical, BLUE-BLACK with IODINE (classic starch test); (2) AMYLOPECTIN (75-80%) — branched α-1,4 + α-1,6 chains; iodine-brown. STORED in AMYLOPLASTS (non-pigmented plastids) of: (a) TUBERS (potato, tapioca); (b) SEEDS (rice, wheat, maize, barley, pulses); (c) ROOTS (sweet potato, yam, carrot); (d) CORMS (colocasia, onion); (e) LEAVES as 'transient starch' during the day (used up at night). In ANIMALS: equivalent is GLYCOGEN (liver + muscle). Non-animal cellular storage also includes: (f) INULIN in dahlia tubers + Jerusalem artichoke — fructose polymer (prebiotic fibre). DIGESTION: starch → maltose (by amylase enzyme in saliva + pancreas) → glucose (by maltase in small intestine brush border) → absorbed to blood. STARCH TEST: iodine (I₂ in KI) turns starch DEEP BLUE-BLACK — a classic visual test. Used in biology lab + to detect leaked boiled rice/pasta water. CELLULOSE — other major plant polysaccharide; β-1,4 linked glucose; STRUCTURAL (cell walls), not storage; NOT digestible by humans (we lack cellulase; ruminants + termites have symbiotic microbes). Plant fibres (cotton, linen, jute) = mostly cellulose. NOT STORED as free glucose (osmotic burden — cells would burst). Humans store glucose as GLYCOGEN in liver (~100g) + muscles (~400g); extras converted to FAT.

questions.stem: Nearly HALF of global photosynthesis occurs in:

options.option_text: OCEANS — carried out by PHYTOPLANKTON (cyanobacteria, diatoms, dinoflagellates, etc.); they produce ~50% of Earth's atmospheric O₂

questions.explanation: OCEANIC PHOTOSYNTHESIS — ~50% of global photosynthesis + O₂ production is by MARINE PHYTOPLANKTON, not terrestrial forests. PHYTOPLANKTON — microscopic drifting photosynthetic organisms in top 100m of oceans + lakes: (a) CYANOBACTERIA (Prochlorococcus + Synechococcus — Prochlorococcus alone may be the most abundant photosynthetic organism on Earth, ~10²⁷ cells); (b) DIATOMS (glass-shelled algae, SiO₂ frustules; dominant in cold + nutrient-rich waters; deposit 'diatomaceous earth' on ocean floor over geological time); (c) DINOFLAGELLATES (some cause red tides — harmful algal blooms); (d) COCCOLITHOPHORES (CaCO₃-plated, contribute to ocean carbonate; their fossils built the WHITE CLIFFS of Dover). FOOD WEB: phytoplankton → zooplankton (copepods, krill) → small fish → large fish → top predators + seabirds + whales. LITTLE ANIMALS FISHED: KRILL (Antarctic) is the base of the Antarctic food web. CLIMATE ROLE: phytoplankton's CARBON PUMP moves CO₂ from atm to deep sea — responsible for the 'biological pump' (~11 Gt C/yr sinks to depth as marine snow). DIMS (dimethyl sulphide) from phytoplankton becomes cloud-nucleating aerosols, influencing climate. STROMATOLITES — fossil cyanobacterial mats — earliest life evidence (3.5 Ga, Australia). ORIGIN of OXYGEN: cyanobacteria first 'invented' oxygenic photosynthesis ~2.7 Ga; Great Oxidation Event 2.4 Ga. MODERN THREATS: ocean warming + acidification (CO₂ dissolves → carbonic acid, lowering pH; affects calcifiers like coccolithophores + coral). Coral reefs are declining (2024-25 5th GLOBAL MASS BLEACHING EVENT declared by NOAA + ICRI — worst on record).
